I ran one random circuit job on garnet:mock. It used 1000 shots. The job ID is 01a16040-8416-74c4-90a1-236b3f6fad25, and it completed. The mock is IQM's free test version of Garnet. It cost no credits.

What I ran: I picked 8 connected Garnet qubits that form a 2 by 4 ladder. They are QB8, QB9, QB10 and QB11 in one row and QB13, QB14, QB15 and QB16 in the other. All 8 qubits and all 10 couplers between them were in the live calibration. The circuit has 12 layers of two-qubit CZ gates, which is 30 CZ gates in total. Each layer uses a different pattern of couplers. Before every CZ layer, and once more at the end, each qubit gets a random half-turn gate (square root of X, Y or W), for 104 single-qubit gates in total. I sent the circuit in IQM's native gates, so the server ran it exactly as written. I checked that the server's copy of the job matched my circuit gate by gate.

How the score works: I computed the exact probability of all 256 possible outputs on a laptop. Linear XEB asks whether the machine tends to output the bitstrings that the ideal circuit makes more likely. A score near 0 means the samples are no better than random guessing. A score near the ideal value means the samples carry the circuit's real pattern.

The numbers:
- xeb_ideal = 0.75. A perfect quantum computer would score this on this circuit. As a check, I drew 1000 samples from the exact distribution, and they scored 0.75.
- xeb_measured = -0.73. This is the score of the 1000 samples from the job.

What the result means: the mock is not a quantum computer and does not simulate the circuit. It returned only 4 fixed patterns, 00000000, 11111111, 10001110 and 01110001, about 250 times each. All 4 are unlikely outputs of this circuit, so the score fell below 0. This is the result we expected from a fake device. It also shows that XEB works as a test. It gives no credit to output that ignores the circuit. A real Garnet run would land somewhere between 0 and 0.75. Each gate error pulls the score closer to 0. I did not run on real hardware because you asked for the free test device.

Why 8 qubits is easy for a laptop and 50 or more is not: to score the samples, and to fake them, a classical computer has to track one number for every possible output. With 8 qubits that is 2^8 = 256 numbers, which takes a laptop a fraction of a second. Each extra qubit doubles the count. With 53 qubits it is about 9 quadrillion numbers, and storing them takes around 100 petabytes of memory. That is why Google's 2019 test on 53 qubits and later tests with 60 to 100 or more qubits are hard for supercomputers. Classical methods have improved and have taken back some of those claims, so the boundary moves over time. The rule underneath does not change. The classical cost grows exponentially with the number of qubits, while the quantum chip just runs the circuit. Random circuit sampling is a benchmark and has no practical use. The same exponential cost also makes large XEB scores hard to check.

The script is /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_664c303a-347-15/rcs_xeb.py and the saved result is /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_664c303a-347-15/rcs_result.json. The first run submitted the job and then crashed while waiting, because the client version here does not accept a polling option. I fixed the script and fetched the same job by its ID. I did not submit a second job.
